t: Compare Strings by Frequency of the Smallest Character
o:
For each string, f(s) is the count of its lexicographically smallest character. For every query we must count how many words have a strictly larger f value. With n = 2000 words and m = 2000 queries, even an O(n·m) brute force (4000·10 character scans) fits easily. The key observation: since strings have length ≤ 10, f(s) is always between 1 and 10, so we can bucket word frequencies and answer each query in O(1) with prefix sums — or sort the frequencies and binary search.

Example 1: f("cbd")=1 ('c' appears once), f("zaaaz")=3 ('a' appears three times), so 1 < 3 → answer [1]. Example 2: f values of words are [1,2,3,4]; query "bbb" has f=1, only 4 > 1 → 1; query "cc" has f=2, both 3 and 4 exceed it → 2.
k: f(s) depends only on string length ≤ 10, so f(s) ∈ [1, 10] — tiny value range enables counting/bucketing.
Each query asks for a count of values strictly greater than f(query), which is a classic 'sort + upper bound' or 'prefix sum from above' problem.
Computing f(s) is O(len): find the smallest character, then count it.

a.i: Directly compute f for every word once, then for each query compute f(queries[i]) and linearly scan all stored word frequencies counting those strictly greater. This works because constraints are small (≤ 2000 × 2000 comparisons).
s: Define f(s): find min character, count its occurrences in one pass.
Precompute freq[w] = f(w) for all words.
For each query q, compute fq = f(q).
Count how many freq[w] > fq; append to answer.
a.t: O((n + m) · L + n · m) where L ≤ 10 is max string length — computing all f values is linear, then each of m queries scans n word frequencies.
a.sp: O(n) to store the precomputed word frequencies.

a.n: Approach 2: Sort Word Frequencies + Binary Search
a.i: Sort the array of word frequencies. For a query with frequency fq, the number of words with frequency strictly greater than fq equals n minus the index of the first element greater than fq (upper bound via bisect_right / upper_bound). Each query then costs O(log n) instead of O(n).
s: Compute f(w) for every word and sort the resulting array.
Compute fq = f(q) for each query.
Binary search for the first index with value > fq (bisect_right on sorted list).
Answer is n minus that index.
a.t: O((n + m) · L + n log n + m log n) — sorting the n frequencies dominates preprocessing; each query does one O(log n) binary search.
a.sp: O(n) for the sorted frequency array.

a.i: Since string length ≤ 10, every f value lies in [1, 10]. Build a count array over these 11 buckets, then compute suffix sums so that suf[v] = number of words with frequency ≥ v. Each query is answered in O(1) as suf[fq + 1]. This removes sorting entirely.
s: Build cnt[1..10] where cnt[v] = number of words with f(w) = v.
Build suffix sums: suf[v] = cnt[v] + suf[v+1], suf[11] = 0.
For each query, compute fq = f(q).
If fq == 10 answer 0, else answer suf[fq + 1].
a.t: O((n + m) · L) — one pass over all strings to compute f values plus O(10) suffix-sum work; no sorting needed.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — two fixed-size arrays of length 12.

w: In an interview, start with the brute force to show correctness, then mention that f values are bounded by 10 and pivot to either binary search or the counting/suffix-sum trick. The suffix-sum approach is optimal and simplest to code correctly. Pitfalls: using strict inequality (count only frequencies strictly greater than the query's), off-by-one when indexing the suffix array (use fq + 1, and note fq can be 10 so the array needs size 11–12), and forgetting that f counts occurrences of the minimum character, not just returns 1. Likely follow-ups: what if string lengths were unbounded (then sort + binary search generalizes better than fixed buckets), or if you needed counts per range rather than 'greater than'.
